tips.greetings: 💡 Saying Sumimasen first (excuse me) before any request is the polite way to get someone's attention.
tips.food: 💡 Many ramen shops use vending machines at the entrance — buy your ticket before sitting. Slurping noodles is a compliment.
tips.directions: 💡 Japanese addresses work by block, not street name. Always save your destination in Google Maps before leaving your hotel.
tips.numbers: 💡 Japanese uses two number systems. Ichi, ni, san (Chinese-origin) works for almost all travel situations.
tips.emergency: 💡 Police: 110. Fire & Ambulance: 119. Police boxes (koban) are everywhere and officers are helpful.
tips.shopping: Do not bargain, and do not tip. Tax-free counters need your passport.
tips.medical: Call 119 for an ambulance. A koban police box can point you to a clinic.
tips.immigration: Have the address of your first hotel. Fingerprints are taken at the border.
tips.hotel: Shoes come off in the entrance. Shared baths may refuse tattoos.
tips.transport: Load a Suica or Pasmo at the airport station. Train doors close on time.

pronGuide.title: Japanese Sounds
tips: Each mora (syllable unit) gets equal time — no heavy stress
Double consonants (kk, tt, ss) get a brief pause before them
R is between English L and R — tongue tip near the roof of the mouth
Long vowels (aa, oo, uu) are held twice as long as short ones

culture.note: A small nod works for tourists. A deeper bow shows more respect. Handshakes are uncommon — let locals lead.
Eating on the go is considered rude. Finish your food at the stall or find a bench. Exception: festival (matsuri) food stalls.
No phone calls on trains. Keep voices low. Phones on silent or vibrate — it's an unspoken rule everyone follows.
Japan is surprisingly cash-heavy. Many restaurants, small shops, and temples don't accept cards. Keep ¥5,000–10,000 on you.
Bins are rare outside convenience stores and train stations. Carry your rubbish — everyone does.
Shower thoroughly before entering the communal bath. Tattoos are banned at most onsens — check in advance.

money.note: Many izakayas, ramen shops, and smaller restaurants are cash only. Keep ¥5,000–10,000 at all times.

money.rule: 7-Eleven and Japan Post ATMs are your friends
money.note: These accept foreign cards with fair fees (~¥220/withdrawal). Take out more at once to minimise charges.
Loaded via iPhone Wallet or at station machines. Used on all trains, buses, and convenience stores across Japan.
Non-resident visitors get 10% consumption tax back at department stores and electronics shops — show your passport.
Tipping is not just unnecessary — it can genuinely confuse or embarrass service staff. Great service is simply expected.

food.name: Ramen
food.what: Regional broth-based noodle soup — tonkotsu (Hakata), miso (Sapporo), shoyu (Tokyo)
food.tip: Follow the locals and use the vending machine to order. Eat it hot and finish quickly.

food.name: Kaiten-zushi
food.what: Conveyor belt sushi — affordable, fun, and surprisingly high quality at chain restaurants like Sushiro
food.tip: Plates are colour-coded by price. Order hot items via the touchscreen tablet.

food.name: Takoyaki
food.what: Osaka street food — octopus-filled batter balls topped with mayo, bonito flakes, and takoyaki sauce
food.tip: Blow on them — they stay piping hot inside long after the outside cools.

food.name: Convenience store food
food.what: 7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart onigiri, sandwiches, and hot foods are genuinely delicious
food.tip: Onigiri (rice balls) make perfect cheap breakfasts. The tuna mayo is a classic.

food.name: Matcha everything
food.what: Green tea flavour in ice cream, KitKats, lattes, cakes — uniquely Japanese and worth trying
food.tip: Uji (near Kyoto) is Japan's matcha heartland for the most authentic versions.

food.name: Japanese whisky
food.what: World-class single malts from Nikka and Suntory — smoother and more delicate than Scotch
food.tip: Try it at a whisky bar in Ginza or Shinjuku. Prices are much better than buying abroad.

safety.note: One of the world's safest countries. Violent crime targeting tourists is virtually unheard of.

safety.rule: Lost items are almost always returned
safety.note: Leave something on a train or in a café — go back and it will almost certainly still be there or handed to staff.
Download the NHK World app for earthquake alerts. Know your hotel's evacuation plan. Keep shoes near your bed.
Casino gambling is technically illegal (though being liberalised). Pachinko parlours are loud and smoky — enter with curiosity.
Making or receiving calls on public transport is a social no-no. Text instead. Priority seats are for elderly and pregnant — vacate immediately.

apps.desc: Free cancellation filters are essential in Japan where plans can change.
